questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What sets the internal energy of an ideal gas
questions.learningObjective: state that the internal energy of an ideal gas depends on temperature alone
questions.stem: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, which single quantity completely determines the internal energy of the gas?

options.misconception: believes the volume term in the equation of state sets U
thinks U is a function of the mechanical state variables

options.text: The work the gas has done
options.misconception: believes stored energy depends on the path taken

questions.explanation: Joule's law says the internal energy of an ideal gas is a function of temperature alone, because for a monatomic gas U = (3/2)nRT and no other quantity appears. At 300 K one mole holds 1.5 x 8.314 J/(mol K) x 300 K = 3741 J whether it fills 0.0249 m3 at 1.00e5 Pa or 0.0499 m3 at 5.00e4 Pa. The trap is the pressure or volume pair, which do change U for a real gas but leave an ideal one untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what the microscopic energy of an ideal gas depends on.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Internal energy of a monatomic gas
questions.learningObjective: compute the internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas from its amount and temperature
questions.stem: A sample contains 2.00 mol of a monatomic ideal gas at 400 K. Taking the universal gas constant as 8.314 J per mol per kelvin, what is the internal energy of the sample in joules? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: For a monatomic ideal gas U = (3/2)nRT = 1.5 x 2.00 mol x 8.314 J/(mol K) x 400 K = 9977 J. Check the other way: the molar heat capacity at constant volume is Cv = 3R/2 = 12.47 J/(mol K), so heating from absolute zero gives U = nCvT = 2.00 x 12.47 x 400 = 9977 J, the same number. The trap is (5/2)nRT, the diatomic value, which gives 1.66e4 J by wrongly counting rotational degrees of freedom.
questions.hint: Monatomic means three translational degrees of freedom per atom.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Molar heat capacity at constant volume
questions.learningObjective: state the molar heat capacity at constant volume of a monatomic ideal gas
questions.stem: What is the molar heat capacity at constant volume of a monatomic ideal gas, in joules per mole per kelvin?

options.misconception: quotes the constant-pressure value instead
counts the diatomic rotational degrees of freedom
quotes the gas constant with no degree-of-freedom factor

questions.explanation: Three translational degrees of freedom put half kT into each quadratic term, so Cv = 3R/2 = 3 x 8.314 / 2 = 12.47 J/(mol K), which rounds to 12.5. Check the other way: the adiabatic index is gamma = 5/3, so Cp = gammaCv = 1.667 x 12.47 = 20.8 J/(mol K), the known constant-pressure value, and Cp - Cv = 8.314 leaves exactly the gas constant. The trap is 20.8, which is Cp rather than Cv, or 25.0, the diatomic value 5R/2.
questions.hint: Count the translational degrees of freedom, then halve the gas constant per degree.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why no work is done at constant volume
questions.learningObjective: explain why the first law reduces to a statement about internal energy at constant volume
questions.stem: A gas sample is heated inside a rigid sealed tank. Why does the first law for that sample reduce to a statement about internal energy alone?

options.text: The walls do not move, so the gas does no work on its surroundings
The tank is insulated, so no heat can reach the gas at all
options.misconception: confuses a rigid container with a thermally sealed one

options.text: The pressure rises, so the work done by the gas is zero
options.misconception: believes rising pressure cancels the work term

options.text: The tank is sealed, so the amount of gas cannot change
options.misconception: makes a statement about amount in place of one about work

questions.explanation: Work is the integral of pressure over the change in volume, W = the integral of P dV, and a rigid tank has dV = 0 everywhere, so W = 0 and the first law becomes delta U = Q. Heating 1.00 mol of monatomic gas by 100 K then needs Q = nCv delta T = 12.47 J/(mol K) x 100 K = 1247 J, all of it landing as internal energy. The trap is the insulation answer, which is about heat flow rather than the volume term, and the sealed-tank answer, which says nothing about work at all.
questions.hint: Look at the work term in the first law and what volume change would be needed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Temperature change from the first law
questions.learningObjective: obtain a temperature change from heat supplied and work done
questions.stem: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. By how many kelvins does the temperature of the gas change? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J per mol per kelvin and report the number only.
questions.explanation: The first law is delta U = Q - W = 500 J - 200 J = 300 J, and for a monatomic gas delta U = nCv delta T with Cv = 3R/2 = 12.47 J/(mol K), so delta T = 300 J / (1.00 mol x 12.47 J/(mol K)) = 24.1 K. Check the other way: the direct form (3/2)nR delta T = 1.5 x 1.00 x 8.314 x delta T = 300 J gives delta T = 24.06 K, the same value. The trap is adding the two energies to reach 700 J, which overstates the rise because the 200 J of work left the system.
questions.hint: Work done by the gas leaves it, so subtract it from the heat absorbed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Heat needed for constant-pressure heating
questions.learningObjective: compute the heat required for a constant-pressure temperature change
questions.stem: One mole of a monatomic ideal gas is heated from 300 K to 400 K while the pressure is held constant. What heat must be supplied, in joules? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J per mol per kelvin and report the number only.
questions.explanation: At constant pressure the gas expands, so part of the heat does work, and the heat is measured by Cp = 5R/2 = 20.79 J/(mol K): Q = nCp delta T = 1.00 mol x 20.79 J/(mol K) x 100 K = 2079 J. Check the other way through the energy balance: delta U = 1.5 x 1.00 x 8.314 x 100 = 1247 J and W = P delta V = nR delta T = 831 J, and 1247 J + 831 J = 2079 J. The trap is 1247 J, the constant-volume value, which forgets the 831 J of expansion work.
questions.hint: Use the heat capacity appropriate to constant pressure, not constant volume.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Expansion work at constant pressure
questions.learningObjective: compute the expansion work of an ideal gas at constant pressure
questions.stem: One mole of an ideal gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.00e5 Pa as its temperature rises from 300 K to 400 K. What work does the gas do on its surroundings, in joules? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J per mol per kelvin and report the number only.
questions.explanation: From PV = nRT at constant pressure, delta V = nR delta T / P, so W = P delta V = nR delta T = 1.00 mol x 8.314 J/(mol K) x 100 K = 831 J. Check the other way through the first law: the constant-pressure heat is 2079 J and delta U = 1.5 x 1.00 x 8.314 x 100 = 1247 J, so the work must be Q - delta U = 2079 J - 1247 J = 832 J, which rounds to the same 831 J. The trap is 1247 J, the internal energy rise, which is not the work at all.
questions.hint: Use the ideal gas law to get the volume change, then multiply by the pressure.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Heat capacities differ by the gas constant
questions.learningObjective: obtain one heat capacity from the other using the gas constant
questions.stem: A gas sample is measured to have a molar heat capacity at constant pressure of 29.1 J per mol per kelvin. What is its molar heat capacity at constant volume, in joules per mole per kelvin?

options.misconception: borrows the monatomic value instead of using the measurement
adds the gas constant instead of subtracting it
returns the gas constant as if it were the heat capacity

questions.explanation: For any ideal gas Cp - Cv = R, so Cv = 29.1 - 8.314 = 20.79, about 20.8 J/(mol K), which is the 5R/2 of a diatomic gas. Check the other way: adding R back, 20.79 + 8.314 = 29.1 J/(mol K), the measured value, and the ratio 29.1/20.79 = 1.40 is the diatomic adiabatic index 7/5. The trap is 12.5, the monatomic Cv, which would need a Cp of 20.8 and so belongs to a different gas entirely.
questions.hint: The two heat capacities differ by exactly one gas constant.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Adiabatic index of a gas
questions.learningObjective: compute the adiabatic index from measured heat capacities
questions.stem: A gas has a molar heat capacity at constant pressure of 29.1 J per mol per kelvin and one at constant volume of 20.8 J per mol per kelvin. What is the adiabatic index of that gas?

options.misconception: inverts the ratio so the index falls below one
reports the gas constant left over after the subtraction
assumes equal heat capacities for every ideal gas

questions.explanation: The adiabatic index is the ratio gamma = Cp/Cv = 29.1 / 20.8 = 1.40, the 7/5 expected for a diatomic gas with five active degrees of freedom. Check the other way: gamma = 1 + R/Cv = 1 + 8.314/20.8 = 1 + 0.400 = 1.40, the same value, and this second form shows why gamma must exceed one, since the gas constant is positive. The trap is 0.71, the reciprocal, which would claim Cp is smaller than Cv and is impossible for a real gas.
questions.hint: Take the ratio of the two measured heat capacities.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Why the change in internal energy is path independent
questions.learningObjective: explain why two different paths between the same states give the same internal energy change
questions.stem: A gas sample is taken from state A to state B first by a slow isothermal expansion and then by a sudden free expansion into a vacuum. Why is the change in internal energy the same for both routes?

options.text: Internal energy is a state function fixed by the endpoints alone
Both routes happen to transfer exactly the same amount of heat
options.misconception: assumes equal heat without checking the work done

options.text: Both routes do exactly the same amount of work on the surroundings
options.misconception: claims equal work where a free expansion does none

options.text: The temperature of the gas is unchanged in both of the routes
options.misconception: assumes the second route is also isothermal

questions.explanation: Internal energy is a state function, so for an ideal gas U = (3/2)nRT depends only on T, and a route from one temperature to the same temperature has the same delta U, namely zero. The heat and work differ wildly: the isothermal step takes in Q = W = nRT ln(V2/V1) = 1.00 x 8.314 x 300 x 0.693 = 1729 J and does the same work back, while the free expansion into a vacuum does no work and absorbs no heat. Since delta U = Q - W is 1729 - 1729 = 0 in one case and 0 - 0 = 0 in the other, only the state-function view explains the match.
questions.hint: Compare the heat and the work in each route, then see what is left over.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Work in an isothermal expansion
questions.learningObjective: compute the work done by an ideal gas in an isothermal expansion
questions.stem: One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K expands isothermally from 0.500 m3 to 1.000 m3. What work does the gas do on its surroundings, in joules? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J per mol per kelvin and report the number only.
questions.explanation: For an isothermal ideal gas delta U = 0, and integrating W = nRT ln(V2/V1) gives 1.00 mol x 8.314 J/(mol K) x 300 K x ln(1.000/0.500) = 2494 J x 0.693 = 1729 J. Check the other way by the pressure form: W = P1V1 ln(V2/V1) = 2494 J x 0.693 = 1729 J, since P1V1 = nRT = 2494 J. Because the temperature never changes, delta U = 0 forces Q = W = 1729 J, so the heat taken in exactly supplies the work done.
questions.hint: Use the logarithmic form of the isothermal work and keep the natural logarithm.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Work in an adiabatic expansion
questions.learningObjective: compute the work of a reversible adiabatic expansion two independent ways
questions.stem: Two moles of a monatomic ideal gas expand adiabatically and reversibly as their temperature falls from 300 K to 240 K. What work does the gas do, in joules? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J per mol per kelvin and the adiabatic index of a monatomic gas as 5 over 3.

options.misconception: forgets to divide by gamma minus one
doubles the temperature span instead of using 60 K
treats the energy loss as work done on the gas

questions.explanation: The reversible adiabatic work is W = (P1V1 - P2V2)/(gamma - 1). With P1V1 = nRT1 = 2.00 x 8.314 x 300 = 4988 J and P2V2 = 2.00 x 8.314 x 240 = 3991 J, the difference of 998 J divided by 5/3 - 1 = 0.667 gives 1497 J. Check the other way, which needs no pressure at all: the gas is insulated so delta U = -W, and delta U = (3/2)nR(T2 - T1) = 1.5 x 2.00 x 8.314 x (-60) = -1497 J, so W = +1497 J. The trap is a positive internal energy change, which would mean the gas heated while expanding with no heat supplied.
questions.hint: Set up the adiabatic work twice, once with pressures and once with temperatures.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Volume from the ideal gas law
questions.learningObjective: solve the ideal gas law for the volume of a gas sample
questions.stem: One mole of an ideal gas is held at a pressure of 1.00e5 Pa and a temperature of 300 K. What volume does it fill, in cubic metres? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J per mol per kelvin and report the number only.
questions.explanation: Rearranging PV = nRT gives V = nRT/P = 1.00 mol x 8.314 J/(mol K) x 300 K / 1.00e5 Pa = 2494 J / 1.00e5 Pa = 0.0249 m3. Check the other way: n = PV/(RT) = 1.00e5 Pa x 0.0249 m3 / (8.314 J/(mol K) x 300 K) = 2490 J / 2494 J = 0.998 mol, which is the stated one mole to three figures. The trap is 0.00249 m3, which puts the pressure and volume in the wrong order, or 2.49 m3, which forgets to divide by the pressure at all.
questions.hint: Rearrange the ideal gas law so the volume stands on its own.

questions.topic: Pressure from the ideal gas law
questions.learningObjective: solve the ideal gas law for the pressure of a gas sample
questions.stem: A rigid tank of volume 0.0250 m3 holds 1.00 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K. What pressure does the gas exert, in pascals? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J per mol per kelvin and report the number only.
questions.explanation: Solving PV = nRT for the pressure gives P = nRT/V = 1.00 mol x 8.314 J/(mol K) x 300 K / 0.0250 m3 = 2494 J / 0.0250 m3 = 9.977e4 Pa. Check the other way: P times V = 9.977e4 Pa x 0.0250 m3 = 2494 J, which equals nRT = 1.00 x 8.314 x 300 = 2494 J, so the product matches from either side. The trap is 2.494e6 Pa, which forgets to divide by the volume, or 2.00e4 Pa, which treats 0.0250 as 0.125.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Pressure response of a rigid tank to heating
questions.learningObjective: interpret two pressure readings in a fixed-volume tank to extract the pressure-temperature relation
questions.stem: A rigid tank of volume 0.0250 m3 holding 1.00 mol of gas is recorded in two states: 300 K with a pressure of 1.00e5 Pa, and 450 K with a pressure of 1.50e5 Pa. What do these two readings show about the pressure in this tank?

options.text: The pressure is proportional to the kelvin temperature, so 450 over 300 gives 1.50
The pressure is proportional to the inverse temperature, falling on heating
options.misconception: inverts the pressure-temperature relation at fixed volume

options.text: The pressure is unchanged, so the extra heat all left as work
options.misconception: assumes work happens in a tank whose walls cannot move

options.text: The pressure rises fourfold, tracking the square of the temperature
options.misconception: expects a squared rather than a linear dependence on T

questions.explanation: With volume and amount fixed, PV = nRT reduces to P/T = nR/V, a constant, so 1.00e5 Pa / 300 K = 333 Pa per kelvin and 1.50e5 Pa / 450 K = 333 Pa per kelvin, the same number. Check the other way: back out the amount of gas, n = PV/(RT) = 1.00e5 x 0.0250/(8.314 x 300) = 1.00 mol at the first state and 1.50e5 x 0.0250/(8.314 x 450) = 1.00 mol at the second, unchanged. The trap is the inverse pair, which would predict the pressure falling while the tank is heated.
questions.hint: Divide the pressure by the temperature in each state and compare the two results.

questions.topic: Isothermal compression
questions.learningObjective: apply the constant-temperature form of the ideal gas law
questions.stem: A gas sample at 300 K has a pressure of 2.00e5 Pa in a volume of 0.0100 m3. It is compressed isothermally until the volume is 0.0200 m3. What is the new pressure, in pascals?

options.misconception: assumes the pressure cannot change at constant temperature
scales the pressure with the volume instead of inversely
applies the compression ratio a second time

Check the other way: 1.00e5 Pa x 0.0200 m3 = 2000 J and 2.00e5 Pa x 0.0100 m3 = 2000 J, the two products being equal as required. The trap is 4.00e5 Pa, which scales the pressure with the volume instead of inversely, or 5.00e4 Pa, which uses the ratio of volumes twice.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Reading a pressure-volume table for a sealed sample
questions.learningObjective: infer from a table of readings whether the amount of gas has changed
questions.stem: For a sealed gas sample three states are recorded: 1.00e5 Pa with 0.0250 m3 at 300 K, 2.00e5 Pa with 0.0125 m3 at 300 K, and 5.00e4 Pa with 0.0500 m3 at 300 K. What do these three rows show?

options.text: PV is the same in all three rows, so the amount of gas is constant
P and V are both constant, so the temperature must be rising
options.misconception: claims two changing columns are in fact constant

options.text: V doubles from row to row, so the amount of gas is doubling
options.misconception: reads a volume change as an amount change

options.text: P varies but V does not, so the gas is leaking out of the tank
options.misconception: invents a leak where both columns do change

Check the other way: the first and last rows differ by a factor of two in pressure and a factor of two in volume, so n is untouched. The trap is the leaking answer, which would need the product PV to fall, not stay put.

questions.topic: What an isochoric process holds fixed
questions.learningObjective: identify the quantity held constant in an isochoric process
questions.stem: In an isochoric process on a gas sample, which quantity is deliberately held at a constant value throughout?

options.misconception: confuses isochoric with isobaric
confuses isochoric with isothermal

options.text: The internal energy of the gas
options.misconception: assumes a fixed volume implies a fixed temperature

questions.explanation: The prefix iso means equal and the suffix choric means volume, so an isochoric process holds V constant, and with n also fixed that leaves P/T constant rather than P or T. Heating 1.00 mol from 300 K to 400 K in a 0.0250 m3 tank therefore raises the pressure from 9.98e4 Pa by the factor 400/300 = 1.33, and the gas does no work on its surroundings. The trap is the isobaric answer, which is a different process, and the constant-temperature answer, which is isothermal.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: What makes a process adiabatic
questions.learningObjective: state the defining condition of an adiabatic process and its consequence for internal energy
questions.stem: A cylinder of gas expands rapidly and drives a piston with no time for heat to flow between the gas and its surroundings. Which statement holds throughout that expansion?

options.text: The heat transfer is zero, so any work done lowers the internal energy
The temperature is unchanged, so the internal energy stays the same

options.text: The pressure and volume are both constant, so no work is done

questions.topic: Degrees of freedom of a diatomic gas
questions.learningObjective: count the degrees of freedom that set the molar heat capacity of a diatomic gas

adds vibrational modes that are frozen out at room temperature
counts the rotations alone and drops all translation

questions.learningObjective: compute the root-mean-square molecular speed from the molar mass and temperature
questions.stem: Nitrogen of molar mass 0.0280 kg per mole is at 300 K. What is the root-mean-square speed of its molecules, in metres per second? Take the gas constant as 8.314 J per mol per kelvin and report the number only.
questions.explanation: The root-mean-square speed is v = the square root of 3RT/M, so v = the square root of 3 x 8.314 J/(mol K) x 300 K / 0.0280 kg/mol = the square root of 267236 = 517 m/s. Check the other way with a single molecule: its mass is 0.0280 kg/mol / 6.022e23 per mol = 4.65e-26 kg, and v = the square root of 3kT/m = the square root of 3 x 1.381e-23 x 300 / 4.65e-26 = the square root of 267290 = 517 m/s, the same speed. The trap is 298 m/s, the mean speed that involves pi, or 267236 m/s, which forgets the square root.
questions.hint: Three times the gas constant times the temperature, over the molar mass, then square-rooted.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: How the molecular speed scales with temperature
questions.learningObjective: determine how the molecular speed of a fixed gas changes with temperature
questions.stem: A gas of unchanged identity is heated from 300 K to 600 K. By what factor does the root-mean-square speed of its molecules increase?

options.misconception: scales the speed in direct proportion to temperature
treats the mean kinetic energy itself as the speed
assumes molecular speed does not depend on temperature

questions.explanation: With M fixed, v = the square root of 3RT/M depends on the square root of the absolute temperature, so the factor is the square root of 600/300 = the square root of 2 = 1.41. Check the other way with the numbers: at 300 K the nitrogen speed is 517 m/s, and at 600 K it is the square root of 3 x 8.314 x 600 / 0.0280 = the square root of 534471 = 731 m/s, and 731/517 = 1.41. The trap is 2.00, which would follow if v were proportional to T, and 4.00, which treats the kinetic energy as the speed.
questions.hint: The speed depends on the square root of the absolute temperature, not on the temperature itself.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Effect of adding gas at fixed volume
questions.learningObjective: determine how the pressure responds to a change in the amount of gas at fixed volume and temperature
questions.stem: A rigid tank of volume 0.0250 m3 holds gas at 300 K. The amount of gas is doubled while the temperature and the volume stay unchanged. What happens to the pressure?

options.misconception: assumes more particles mean fewer collisions per unit area
forgets that the walls are fixed and cannot give way
applies a squared scaling to a linear relation

questions.explanation: With n, V, and T all but n fixed, PV = nRT makes the pressure directly proportional to the amount of gas, so doubling n doubles P from 9.98e4 Pa to 2.00e5 Pa. Check the other way: n = PV/(RT) at the doubled state gives 2.00e5 x 0.0250/(8.314 x 300) = 5000/2494 = 2.00 mol, twice the original one mole. The trap is the quadrupled answer, which confuses doubling the particle count with a squared effect, and the unchanged answer, which ignores the fixed walls.
questions.hint: Everything on the right-hand side of the gas law is fixed except the amount of gas.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Work read from a pressure-volume diagram
questions.learningObjective: obtain the work from the area under a horizontal path on a pressure-volume diagram
questions.stem: A pressure-volume diagram, with pressure on the vertical axis and volume on the horizontal axis, shows two states joined by a horizontal arrow drawn at a pressure of 2.00e5 Pa, running to the right from 0.0100 m3 to 0.0200 m3. What work does the gas do along that path?

options.misconception: uses half the volume change in the area calculation
doubles the volume change instead of using it directly
multiplies by the pressure alone and drops the volume

questions.explanation: Work is the area under the path on a pressure-volume diagram, and a horizontal path is an isobaric expansion, so W = P delta V = 2.00e5 Pa x (0.0200 - 0.0100) m3 = 2.00e5 x 0.0100 = 2.00e3 J. Check the other way through the ideal gas law: from PV = nRT the product rises from 2000 J to 4000 J, a doubling of the temperature, and for 1.00 mol that is 241 K to 481 K, so nR delta T = 8.314 x 241 = 2.00e3 J, the same work. The trap is 1.00e3 J, which uses half the volume change.
questions.hint: The area under the line is the pressure times the change in volume.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Which segment of a diagram does no work
questions.learningObjective: identify a zero-work segment and infer the temperature change along it from a diagram
questions.stem: A pressure-volume diagram shows state 1 at 1.00e5 Pa and 0.0300 m3, joined to state 2 at 2.00e5 Pa and 0.0300 m3 by a vertical arrow drawn upward, and state 2 joined to state 3 at 2.00e5 Pa and 0.0100 m3 by a horizontal arrow drawn leftward. Which segment does no work on the gas, and what happens to the temperature along it?

options.text: The vertical segment 1 to 2, and the temperature rises there
The vertical segment 1 to 2, and the temperature falls there
options.misconception: expects pressure to fall when volume is unchanged

options.text: The horizontal segment 2 to 3, and the temperature rises there
options.misconception: misses that a horizontal path has no height to form an area

options.text: The horizontal segment 2 to 3, and the temperature falls there
options.misconception: picks the moving-volume segment as the zero-work one

questions.explanation: Work is the area under the path, and the vertical segment from state 1 to state 2 has no horizontal extent, so delta V = 0 and W = 0 however much the pressure doubles. Along it the product PV rises from 1.00e5 x 0.0300 = 3000 J to 2.00e5 x 0.0300 = 6000 J, and nRT tracks that product, so the temperature doubles, from 361 K to 722 K at 1.00 mol. Check the horizontal segment for contrast: delta V = -0.0200 m3 at 2.00e5 Pa, so the gas does -4.00e3 J of work and the product falls from 6000 J to 2000 J.
questions.hint: Work is the area under the path, so look for the segment with no width.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Confusing isothermal with zero heat
questions.learningObjective: diagnose the belief that a constant temperature forbids heat flow
questions.stem: A student writes that because an ideal gas expanding isothermally keeps a constant temperature, no heat can enter or leave it, so Q = 0. What is wrong with the reasoning?

options.text: Constant temperature does not mean zero heat; the heat in equals the work done
Isothermal gases are never allowed to exchange heat with the surroundings
options.misconception: turns a naming convention into a physical prohibition

options.text: The work done in an isothermal expansion is always negative by convention
options.misconception: asserts a sign convention instead of using the first law

options.text: The temperature of a real gas always changes during an isothermal expansion
options.misconception: claims ideal gases are the sole exception to isothermal heating

questions.explanation: Isothermal fixes the temperature, and for an ideal gas that fixes the internal energy, so delta U = 0 and the first law then gives Q = W, not Q = 0. Expanding from 0.500 m3 to 1.000 m3 at 300 K needs Q = W = nRT ln(1.000/0.500) = 1.00 x 8.314 x 300 x 0.693 = 1729 J of heat to arrive. Check the other route: if Q really were zero the balance would give delta U = -W, meaning the gas cooled while doing positive work, which contradicts the constant temperature. The trap is confusing isothermal with adiabatic, whose defining feature really is Q = 0.
questions.hint: Use the first law with delta U = 0 and see what it demands of Q.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Sign of the work term in the first law
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an incorrect sign on the work term of the first law
questions.stem: A gas absorbs 400 J of heat and does 300 J of work by expanding against its surroundings. A student adds the two quantities and reports the internal energy rising by 700 J. What is the error?

options.text: The work term was added; work done by the gas leaves the system
The work term should have been doubled before being added
options.misconception: invents a factor where only a sign is at issue

options.text: The heat term was halved because the gas was expanding
options.misconception: adjusts the heat for a condition that does not change it

options.text: Internal energy cannot change when a gas does positive work
options.misconception: believes positive work freezes the internal energy

questions.explanation: With work defined as done by the gas, the first law is delta U = Q - W, so 400 J - 300 J = 100 J, not 700 J. Check the other way: for 1.00 mol of monatomic gas a 100 J rise means delta T = 100/(1.00 x 12.47) = 8.0 K, whereas a 700 J rise would need 56.1 K, and heating a gas by 56 K at constant volume would need far more than 400 J. The trap is the sign convention itself, which is why texts defining W as work done on the gas write delta U = Q + W and reach the same 100 J.
questions.hint: Ask where the energy that does the work has to go.
